Motivation · 1 of 3 · why now, and why it is worth paying for

The estimated cost of breaking secp256k1 keeps falling — and a chain is permanent

Why a chain cannot wait for the machine

  • The record is permanent. Every signature and every revealed public key stays readable forever — a break applies retroactively to coins already sitting under exposed keys.
  • Changing it is a consensus change, coordinated across a whole network — years, not a software update.

The retirement date is already written down

disallowed
after 2035

cited NIST IR 8547 ipd (Nov 2024), Table 2 — quantum-vulnerable signatures at ≥128-bit strength, which is where secp256k1 sits

Estimates for hardware that does not exist. At one fixed target — RSA-2048 — they fell 20× in six years: the cost falls, not the calendar.

Gidney & Ekerå, Quantum 5:433 (2021) · Gidney, arXiv:2505.15917 (2025) · Babbush et al., IACR ePrint 2026/625 · NIST IR 8547 ipd (2024).

The mechanism · four functions added to a plain signature

Publishing a signature leaks a secret — that is what makes a swap atomic

Both legs settle, or neither does — no trusted third party, and no shared hash lock tying the chains together.

The method · how a basic signature becomes an adaptor signature

One substitution in the challenge hash — the lattice core is reused

Built a second time, independently

C and Rust agree byte for byte on a pinned known-answer digest: b4a10ffb…03be

The digest binds packed outputs over four fixed vectors, not internals; PreVerify and Extract are asserted per vector, not hashed.

Bob learns the witness

his key sk₂ the public lock Y the proof π · 30711–30760 B Alice’s locked signature σ̂₁ · 6736 B the locked signature it made itself the secret y′, extracted
Tries to spend the pre-signature it is holding — ordinary Verify refuses it. Verify(σ̂₁, m₁, pk₁) → ⊥
Needs nothing further from Alice: it reads σ₂ off chain 2, combines it with the σ̂₂ it made itself, then adapts σ̂₁ with what came out and publishes. y′ ← Ext(Y, σ₂, σ̂₂) = z₂ − ẑ₂ σ₁ ← Adapt((Y, y′), pk₁, σ̂₁, m₁) → chain 1
1 · abort gateBob pre-signed only after π and PreVerify(σ̂₁) passed. Neither pre-signature is spendable by anyone.
2 · the tripwireA pre-signature is not a signature — that is what stops Bob claiming early.
3 · publishOn chain it is an ordinary payment: no script, no hash lock, nothing to see.
4 · leak, then claimExt returns y′; Bob adapts σ̂₁ with that value and publishes. Both settle, or neither does.

Step 2 is paired and interleaved against LAS’s own base at identical parameters; the classical ratio is derived from that harness’s means. Step 1’s ×72 is this build’s simplified base (smaller on the FIPS 204 path), and in absolute time a lattice operation is dearer — still under a millisecond.

Rejection attempts are counted, never inferred from timing: 2.615 per Sign against 2.724 per PreSign, and the run aborts unless every timed call matches theory within 5σ.

The lattice signature is payload, not a consensus field — so this venue needs no rule change, and pays in gas instead.

Bitcoin is more restricted — fixed fields, so σ needs a consensus rule. Ethereum is more flexible — contracts, so σ needs a deploy and gas.

Conclusion · the answers, the verdict, and who each one is for

Good enough to build on — what stops deployment is not performance

CAN WE BUILD ONE? — YES, TWICEC ⇆ Rust, byte-identical · zero upstream functions modified
WHAT DOES IT COST? — TIME +8.3%, BYTES ×72and in a whole swap the proof takes 98.6%
WILL A CHAIN TAKE IT? — ETHEREUM: DEPLOY · BITCOIN: NEW RULEcontracts are more flexible · Bitcoin is more restricted, its fields cannot be modified — structural, not a timeline

If you build Bitcoin

Carriage is not the problem. Verification is a consensus rule, not engineering.

  • measured a stock Core v31.1 node already mines these spends — nonstandard to relay, but consensus-valid
  • measured add one rule and a whole two-leg swap settles, against 9 negative controls
  • measured the rule costs 374 µs per input — 11.3× a Schnorr check
  • levels unmatched, so that ratio overstates · the rule is unanalysed — what is missing is analysis, not code

If you build on the EVM

Deployable today, with almost no margin — and no protocol change.

  • measured a real client mined the whole claim in one transaction — 97.8% of the per-transaction cap
  • measured one set down, verification alone is charged 65%
  • derived at the largest set one transaction is exceeded — arithmetic, never a measured total
  • one signature instance, 32-byte message · feasibility is settled, cost is not

If you design the protocol

Budget bytes, not adaptor computation — and budget the proof first.

  • measured the adaptor layer adds at most +8.3% over the base signature
  • measured but its objects are ×72 the classical ones on the wire
  • measured and the proof takes 98.6% of a whole swap — not the signature
  • so the work is π and the statement Y — and a relation whose statement is small by construction

Every figure says which warrant it carries — measured (run 20260804_101750, paired and interleaved, rejection counted and gated to 5σ, C ⇆ Rust byte-identical on digest b4a10ffb…03be), derived, or cited. Anything else is an open question, and is said to be one.
